References & Inspirations
This site’s structure, teaching approach, and visual design are informed by several high-quality textbooks, programming resources, and open-source Quartz-based projects. These references guided both the educational philosophy of the course and the layout of this website.

C++ Programming References

Big C++ by Cay Horstmann
A clear and beginner-friendly textbook that emphasizes practical examples and step-by-step explanations. Several parts of the course’s teaching flow and examples are inspired by this book.
C++ How to Program by Deitel & Deitel
A widely used introductory textbook known for its detailed explanations, example-driven learning, and large collection of practice problems. Its structured progression influenced how topics are introduced throughout this course.
C++ Documentation & Online Tutorials
Supplemental references for syntax details, library functions, and language fundamentals.


Website & Style Inspirations
The styling of this site are inspired by Quartz and several publicly available Quartz-based notes.

Quartz Test Site by fanteastick
github.com/fanteastick/quartz-test
Quartz Setup by bfahrenfort
github.com/bfahrenfort/quartz
Quartz Documentation
Used extensively for structure, navigation, and customization of the site.

These projects helped shape the clean, minimal, and highly navigable design used here.

Course Objectives
The C++ Basic Programming Course introduces students to the foundations of programming through a practical and example-driven approach. With an emphasis on hands-on learning, this course helps students develop algorithmic thinking, write clean and correct C++ programs, and build confidence through structured practice.

Key Elements

Ten Core Sessions: Each session (approx. 3 hours) builds on the previous one, covering essential C++ programming topics in a structured, accessible way.
Optional Enrichment Sessions: Extra workshops on topics such as AI literacy for programmers, debugging techniques, tools, and practical tips for becoming a better developer.
Hands-on Learning: Students write and run code throughout every session, supported by live examples, mini-challenges, and TA feedback.
Fundamental Concepts: Variables, data types, conditionals, loops, functions, arrays, pointers, and an introduction to basic object-oriented thinking.
Algorithmic Thinking: Problem decomposition, tracing, and designing solutions step by step.
Debugging Skills: Understanding compiler errors, runtime issues, and basic debugging tools and strategies.
Clean Coding Practices: Naming, structure, modularity, and writing readable code.
Student-Centered Instruction: Clear explanations, practical exercises, and real-time assistance to address common misunderstandings.


Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:

Write simple and correct C++ programs using fundamental constructs.
Use loops, conditionals, and functions to solve computational problems.
Work with arrays and pointer basics to store and manipulate data.
Trace and debug code effectively.
Apply algorithmic reasoning to break down and implement solutions.
Structure programs cleanly and write readable, maintainable C++ code.
Use the C++ standard library for basic input/output and utility operations.
Build a small terminal-based application that integrates multiple concepts.


Assignments & Workshops
Each week, students will complete hands-on programming assignments based on the topics covered in that week’s workshop(s). These topics include problem solving, data types, control structures, functions, and other fundamental programming concepts.
All assignments will be uploaded to Quera.org, and every student must have an active account.
The assessment process includes:

Automatic evaluation by Quera’s online judge
Manual review by the student’s mentor to ensure

Clean and readable code
Absence of AI-generated or AI-misused content
Proper problem-solving approach
Adherence to course standards



Students will be informed of their scores after review.
Some assignments may include optional bonus problems, which are more challenging and provide extra credit but are not required.
In-Workshop Problems
During each workshop, students will be given approximately three hands-on coding questions.
These will be:

Uploaded to Quera during the workshop
Attempted in class while TAs are available for help
Submitted by the end of the day if not finished during class

These in-workshop tasks help students reinforce the material immediately and get real-time feedback from TAs.

Final Exam
The final exam evaluates the student’s understanding of the fundamental concepts taught throughout the semester.
It will include questions on:

Algorithms
Data types
Control structures
Functions
Arrays
Pointers
Files
Structs
Material covered in the professor’s lectures and slides

Students are expected to demonstrate a clear understanding of how these concepts work and provide correct, well-reasoned solutions to the exam questions.

Final Project
The course culminates in the creation of a terminal-based game, optionally using Unicode characters to enhance the visual experience. Students work in groups of two, applying the full range of skills they’ve learned to design and implement a playable, interactive project.
Previous final projects have included:

Pacman
Tetris
Space Invaders

Requirements typically include:

Clear input/output and user interaction
Use of loops, conditionals, and functions
Arrays and/or pointers for game state management
Modular and well-structured code
Consistent gameplay logic and proper handling of game rules

Students submit:

The complete source code
A short project description
Sample runs or screenshots

Grading
The course grade will be based on three components:

10 points — Assignments & Workshops (combined)
5 points — Final Project
5 points — Final Exam


Required Tools and Accounts
To fully participate in the course, students must have access to the following:

A C++ compiler — preferably g++ from the GNU Compiler Collection
A code editor or IDE — VS Code with the official C/C++ extension is recommended
A Quera.org account — required for submitting and completing programming assignments and workshop problems
A Telegram account — students must join the course’s official Telegram group for announcements, coordination, and Q&A

🧭 Topic: Problem Solving


                  
                  Quick Overview 
                  
                


This foundational topic introduces the core skill of programming: problem-solving. It’s not about writing code immediately, but about learning how to think logically and systematically. We will explore how to break down complex problems into smaller, manageable steps using a structured approach. By the end of this lecture, students will understand the principles of algorithmic thinking and be able to plan solutions using tools like flowcharts and pseudocode before writing a single line of code.




📌 Covered in This Topic

The Art of Problem Solving: An introduction to planning, creativity, innovation, and clearly defining the cause, goal, and potential solutions to a problem.


  Stages of Algorithmic Thinking: A 7-step logical process for solving problems:

    1.  Define the Problem
    2.  Analyze and Understand
    3.  Identify Potential Solutions
    4.  Evaluate and Choose a Solution
    5.  Plan Actions
    6.  Implement the Code
    7.  Review the Results


  What is an Algorithm? Defining an algorithm as a step-by-step procedure or a recipe for solving a problem.
  Introduction to Flowcharts: Learning to visualize the flow of a solution using standard symbols to represent actions, decisions, and data flow.
  Introduction to Pseudocode: Understanding how to write a plain-language, structured description of an algorithm’s steps before translating it into a programming language.
  Choosing the Best Algorithm: An introduction to the criteria for evaluating different solutions, focusing on time and space efficiency, reliability, and simplicity.

🧭 Topic: Basics of C++ & Data Types


                  
                  Quick Overview 
                  
                


This topic introduces how to compile and run C++ code, basic input/output, variables, built-in data types, and the math library.
By the end, students will be able to write simple C++ programs using variables and standard input/output streams.




📌 Covered in This Topic
Part 1 - Basics of C++

History and Evolution of Computing

Origin of the term computer
Early computing devices
Milestones in computer development


Binary and Logic Fundamentals

Why computers use binary
Boolean logic and logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR)
Truth tables and simple logic circuits
32-bit vs 64-bit systems
Data representation:

Number systems (binary, decimal, hexadecimal)
Signed numbers in binary
Floating-point representation
Character encoding: ASCII and Unicode




Introduction to Programming Languages

From machine code to assembly
Evolution of high-level languages
C++ in context: use cases and characteristics
Low-level vs high-level abstraction


Compilers and Program Execution

How code becomes machine-executable
Compiler vs interpreter
Compilation workflow in C++


First Steps in C++ Programming

Writing and compiling a simple C++ program
Basic input and output (cin, cout)
Adding comments and documentation



Part 2 - Data Types and Variables

Understanding Data in Programming

What is data and how it’s represented in memory
Relationship between data and variables


Variables and Memory Basics

Declaring and initializing variables
Variable scope and lifetime (brief intro)


Fundamental Data Types in C++

Overview of primitive types (int, float, double, char, bool)
Memory sizes and limits of each data type
Signed vs unsigned integers


Integers

Integer arithmetic and overflow behavior
Type modifiers (short, long, unsigned)


Floating-Point Numbers

Representation and precision limits
Common rounding and comparison pitfalls
Differences between float, double, and long double


Characters and Text

Character literals and ASCII table
Escape sequences and their meaning
Brief Introduction to Unicode and text encoding
Working with std::string


Booleans and Logic

Boolean literals and expressions
Type conversions to and from boolean


Constants and Immutability

Declaring constants using const
Benefits of using constants in programs


Type Conversion and Casting

Implicit vs explicit type conversion
static_cast, and C-style casts (intro level)


Assignment and Operators

Simple and compound assignment
Operator precedence overview (intro level)


Naming Conventions and Code Style

Common naming conventions in C++
Writing clean and readable variable names


Math Library Overview

Using <cmath> for basic mathematical operations
Common functions (sqrt, pow, abs, round, etc.)

🧭 Topic: C++ Control Structures


                  
                  Quick Overview 
                  
                


📌 Covered in This Topic
Part 1 - Conditions


Introduction to Control Structures

What are control structures and why they matter
How conditions allow decision-making in programs
Types of control flow in C++:

Sequential
Selection (branching — this lecture’s focus)
Iteration (to be covered later)






Operators and Their Categories


Overview: Operators as tools for computation and logic
Main categories relevant to conditions:

Arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) – for expressions inside conditions
Comparison / Relational operators  ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=


Logical operators (&&, ||, !)
Bitwise operators (intro only) (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>)

Distinguish between bitwise and logical operations
Simple binary truth table demonstration





Boolean Expressions and Truth Evaluation

How C++ evaluates boolean expressions (true, false, 0, non-zero)
Short-circuit evaluation with && and ||
Expression combinations and nested conditions
Boolean variables and expressions (bool is_valid = age > 18;)



Conditional Statements

The if Statement**

Basic syntax and flow
Single-statement vs block ({}) forms
Recommended: always use braces for clarity and safety
Readability and indentation rules


if…elseandelse if Chains

Multi-condition logic
Execution flow and exclusivity (only one branch executes)
Common pitfalls (missing else, overlapping conditions)





Nested if Statements

When to nest vs when to restructure
Clean and readable formatting examples
Introduce the idea of early return or guard clauses as clean code alternatives



The Ternary Operator (?:)**

Syntax and usage
Example: result = (x > 0) ? 1 : -1;
When to use vs when not to use
“Short-hand if” — only for simple assignments or expressions
Readability trade-offs



The switch Statement

Purpose and syntax
Supported data types:

int, char, enum, bool (and C++11 constexpr integral types)
⚠️ Not supported: float, double, string





Case labels and the need for break


Default case and its importance


Fall-through behavior (intentional vs accidental)


Example: menu-based program with switch


Operator Precedence and Associativity**

Order in which operators are evaluated
Why parentheses improve readability and prevent bugs
Quick reference table for comparison, logical, and arithmetic operators
Example comparisons showing subtle precedence mistakes



Clean Code and Best Practices**

Always use braces {} even for single statements
Align and indent consistently
Use descriptive variable and condition names (if (is_authenticated) not if (x))
Avoid deeply nested conditions (refactor with functions or early returns)
Comment why not what
Test all branches (especially edge cases and default paths)




Part 2 - Loops

Introduction to Iteration

Why repetition is needed in programs
The concept of control flow — branching vs looping


The while Loop

Syntax and structure
Flow of control in while
Typical use cases: input validation, sentinel-controlled loops
Common pitfalls (infinite loops, missing updates)


The do-while Loop

Difference between while and do-while (post-test vs pre-test)
When to use do-while (menus, repeated input until valid)


The for Loop

Syntax and structure (initialization, condition, update)
Iterating over numeric ranges
Loop variable scope and lifetime
Variations: multiple initializations, empty components
Using for for counting and fixed iterations


Loop Control Statements

break — exiting early
continue — skipping to next iteration
return in loops
Discuss readability vs misuse of these


Nested Loops

How inner loops behave relative to outer loops
Common examples: printing patterns, working with 2D arrays
Complexity growth and performance intuition (Brief)


Loop Design Patterns

Counter-controlled loops
Sentinel-controlled loops
Flag-controlled loops
Infinite loops with break condition


Order of Execution Recap

Loop initialization → condition check → body → update
Flow diagrams to illustrate control


Best Practices and Clean Code

Avoid “magic numbers” — use constants in loop bounds
Use meaningful variable names (i, j are fine for indices, otherwise be descriptive)
Ensure loops have clear termination conditions
Maintain consistent indentation and brace style


Debugging and Tracing Loops

Using print statements to track variables
Recognizing off-by-one errors

🧭 Topic: Function Basics


                  
                   Quick Overview :
                  
                


This topic introduces functions in C++, why we use them, how they are
defined and called, how parameters and return values work, and how to
write clean, professional function-based code.




📌 Covered in This Topic
Introduction to Functions

What functions are (self-contained blocks of code)
Key goals:

Modularity
Reusability (Write once, use everywhere)
Readability
Debugging & error isolation


Real-world analogy: a “machine” that takes input and produces output

Why We Need Functions

Eliminating repetition (D.R.Y. — Don’t Repeat Yourself)
Breaking problems into sub-problems
Reducing complexity
Abstraction (main doesn’t care how, only what)
Professional collaboration benefits

User-Defined Functions

Anatomy of a function:

Return type
Function name
Parameters
Body


Function lifecycle:

Declaration (prototype)
Definition
Calling


Declaration vs. Definition
Function prototypes and their purpose

Return Types

Allowed return types
Limitation: a function returns only one value
void functions:

Definition and use cases
Using return; as an “exit door”



Parameters & Arguments

Parameter vs. argument (placeholder vs. actual data)
Order and clarity of parameters
Parameter names optional in prototypes
Scope and lifetime of parameters

Scope & Lifetime

Local variables
Global variables:

What they are
Why to avoid them


Static local variables
Variable shadowing
Priority of scopes

Default Arguments

Syntax of default parameters
Rules:

Must be placed on the right
Evaluated at compile time


Correct vs. incorrect usage
Common ambiguity problems

Parameter Passing Methods

Pass by value

Copy is made
Original variable unchanged
Best for small data types


Pass by reference (&)

Works on original variable
Used for modification or performance


When and why to choose each method

Function Overloading

Definition of overloading
Valid overloading rules
Return type alone does NOT overload
Overload resolution basics
Numeric literal suffixes and their effect
Overloading vs. default arguments (ambiguity)

Clean Code & Best Practices

Syntax and formatting
Function placement & structure
Meaningful naming (verbs for functions)
SRP (Single Responsibility Principle)
Function length and complexity
Refactoring deeply nested logic

🧭 Topic: Recursive Functions


                  
                   Quick Overview :
                  
                


Recursion is a technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that problem, using a base case to stop the process. It’s useful for naturally hierarchical tasks like divide-and-conquer algorithms, backtracking, and tree or graph traversal. While recursion can make code simpler and more intuitive, it also uses more memory and can cause stack overflows if not designed carefully. Choosing recursion vs. iteration depends on the problem’s structure, performance needs, and clarity of the solution.



📌 Covered in This Topic

1. Introduction to Recursion

What recursion means (functions calling themselves)
Real-life analogy (matryoshka dolls / repeated tasks)
Structure of every recursive function (base case + recursive case)


2. How Recursive Functions Are Created

Function call stack review (activation records, return addresses, parameters)
Base cases: preventing infinite recursion
Progress toward the base case (reducing the problem size)
Tracing a simple example (factorial, Fibonacci)


3. Relationship Between Recursion and Iteration

Any recursive solution can be rewritten using loops
Recursion as a conceptual tool vs. iteration as a control-flow tool
Examples:

fibonacci (recursive → iterative)
factorial (recursive → iterative)


When compilers internally convert tail recursion to loops


4. Why Use Recursion? — Problems and Use Cases

Problems naturally defined in terms of smaller subproblems
Divide-and-Conquer algorithms (Merge Sort, Quick Sort)
Backtracking problems (N-Queens, maze solving, subsets/permutations)
Tree/graph traversal (DFS)
Mathematical sequences (Fibonacci, exponentiation)


5. How to Choose Between Recursion and Iteration

Use recursion when the problem is hierarchical, branching, or naturally recursive
Use iteration when performance and memory are critical
Avoid recursion when depth may be very large (risk of stack overflow)
Consider readability vs. efficiency trade-offs


6. Problems With Recursion

High memory usage: stack frames
Stack overflow (deep recursion)
Re-computation of subproblems (e.g., naive Fibonacci)
Harder to debug for beginners
Function call overhead


7. Solutions and Optimizations

Tail Recursion

What tail recursion is
How compilers can optimize it
Example of turning a normal recursion into tail recursion


Memoization

Caching results of recursive calls
When to use it (DP top-down)
Example: optimized Fibonacci




8. Worked Examples

N-Queens (backtracking)
Merge Sort (divide-and-conquer)
Tail-recursive factorial
Memoized Fibonacci

Exactly — you’ve got the concept right! Let’s go step by step, with enough depth for a TA workshop. I’ll explain what a call stack is, what it contains, and how the OS/CPU manages it in memory, keeping it conceptual but technically accurate.

1. What is the Call Stack?


Each running program (process) has a stack segment in its memory layout.


The call stack is a part of that stack segment.


It stores information needed for function calls.


Every time a function is called, a stack frame (activation record) is pushed onto the stack.


When the function returns, the frame is popped.


Stack frames store:


Return address – where to continue after the function finishes


Parameters / arguments – values passed to the function


Local variables – variables declared inside the function


Saved registers / state – CPU registers that need to be restored



2. Stack Memory Management


Stack grows and shrinks automatically as functions are called/returned.


Managed by CPU + OS — the compiler generates instructions to:


Push a new frame when a function is called


Pop the frame when returning




The stack usually grows downwards in memory (from high to low addresses), but this is platform-specific.


Allocation is fast: just move the stack pointer (a CPU register). No heap allocation needed.



3. How a Recursive Function Uses the Stack
Let’s take fact(3) as example:
fact(3) called
fact(2) called
fact(1) called
fact(0) called

Memory perspective (simplified):

























Memory Address (high → low)Content0x7fff…fact(0) frame: n=0, return addr=…0x7fff… - small offsetfact(1) frame: n=1, return addr=…0x7fff… - larger offsetfact(2) frame: n=2, return addr=…0x7fff… - larger offsetfact(3) frame: n=3, return addr=…


Each function call pushes a new frame.


When fact(0) returns, the CPU pops that frame and resumes fact(1).


The stack pointer (SP) register points to the top of the stack at all times.



4. Stack Pointer and Base Pointer
Most CPUs (x86/x64):


SP / RSP (Stack Pointer) → points to the top of the stack


BP / RBP (Base Pointer / Frame Pointer) → fixed reference inside the current frame


Function prologue (simplified):
push rbp       ; save caller's base pointer
mov rbp, rsp   ; set new base pointer for this frame
sub rsp, n     ; allocate space for locals
Function epilogue (simplified):
mov rsp, rbp   ; deallocate locals
pop rbp        ; restore caller's base pointer
ret            ; jump back to return address

5. Stack Overflow


If recursion is too deep, you push more frames than stack space allows.


Result: stack overflow (program crashes).


Typical stack sizes:


Linux: 8 MB (can be changed)


Windows: 1 MB (can be changed)


Example:
void infinite() { infinite(); }
int main() { infinite(); }
This quickly crashes with stack overflow because each call consumes some stack memory.

6. Key Points to Explain to Students


The stack is fast, automatic, LIFO.


Each recursive call gets its own local variables; they do not interfere.


Memory is managed by moving the stack pointer; no malloc/free needed.


Stack is limited → too deep recursion = crash.


Tail recursion can allow compiler optimizations to reuse frames.



7. Optional Visual Analogy


Stack = stack of plates


Each plate = stack frame


Add a plate = push frame


Remove a plate = pop frame


Too many plates = stack overflow



If you want next, I can make a simple diagram-free, code-driven demo that shows:


how stack frames are created


how variables are isolated per frame


how the return addresses “unwind”


This works perfectly for first-term students.

Absolutely! Let’s go step by step, starting from the concept, then the teaching strategy, and finally a set of lecture notes suitable for a TA workshop with first-term CS students. I’ll keep it practical, example-driven, and ready to use.

Backtracking: Concept

1. Definition
Backtracking is a systematic way to explore all possible solutions to a problem by building a solution incrementally and abandoning it (“backtracking”) as soon as it becomes invalid.


Think of it as trying all possibilities in a decision tree, but cutting off branches that cannot lead to a valid solution early.


Backtracking is commonly used in:


N-Queens


Sudoku


Maze solving


Permutations and combinations


Constraint satisfaction problems





2. Key Idea


Start with an empty solution.


Add elements one by one (choices at each step).


Check if the current partial solution is valid:


If yes → proceed recursively to next step.


If no → abandon this branch (backtrack).




Once all steps are tried, return to the previous step and try the next choice.



3. Analogy for Students
Maze Example


You are in a maze: you can go up, down, left, right.


You try one direction:


If you hit a wall → backtrack and try another direction.


If you reach the exit → solution found.




N-Queens Example


Place queens row by row:


Try a column in the current row


If it is safe → move to next row


If no column is safe → backtrack to previous row and try next column





4. Recursive Pattern of Backtracking
A backtracking function generally has this pattern:
void backtrack(currentState) {
    if (solutionIsComplete(currentState)) {
        processSolution(currentState);
        return;
    }
 
    for (choice : allPossibleChoices(currentState)) {
        if (choiceIsValid(currentState, choice)) {
            makeChoice(currentState, choice);  // add choice
            backtrack(currentState);           // recurse
            undoChoice(currentState, choice);  // remove choice (backtrack)
        }
    }
}
Notes:


makeChoice → adds an element to the partial solution


undoChoice → removes it (critical step for backtracking)


Recursive call explores next step



5. Advantages of Backtracking


Finds all possible solutions (not just one).


Efficient because it prunes invalid paths early.


Simple, intuitive recursive implementation.



6. Disadvantages


Can be slow for large input if pruning is insufficient.


Memory usage grows with recursion depth.


Not suitable for very large search spaces without optimizations.



Lecture Notes / Teaching Flow

Slide / Whiteboard Outline
Slide 1: Title & Hook
Title: Backtracking – Systematic Problem Solving
Hook:

“Imagine trying all paths in a maze but leaving immediately when you hit a dead end. That’s backtracking.”


Slide 2: Concept


Definition


Recursive exploration


Pruning invalid paths



Slide 3: Analogy


Maze solving


Stack of choices → “backtrack when blocked”



Slide 4: Recursive Pattern
void backtrack(currentState) {
    if (solutionIsComplete(currentState)) {
        processSolution(currentState);
        return;
    }
 
    for (choice : allPossibleChoices(currentState)) {
        if (choiceIsValid(currentState, choice)) {
            makeChoice(currentState, choice);
            backtrack(currentState);
            undoChoice(currentState, choice);
        }
    }
}


Explain makeChoice and undoChoice clearly


Emphasize that undoing is what “backtracking” literally means



Slide 5: Simple Example
Problem: Place N queens on a chessboard


Try columns in row 0


If safe → move to row 1


If blocked → return to row 0 and try next column


Show partial solution tree:
Row0: Q . .   → continue
Row0: . Q .   → continue
Row0: . . Q   → continue


Draw how the recursion builds and undoes choices


Slide 6: Another Example (Optional)


Maze solving or subset generation


Highlight pruning when path invalid



Slide 7: Important Points


Always check validity before recursing


Always undo changes (backtrack)


Recursion + choice tree = backtracking


Works well with constraints



Slide 8: Practice Exercise


Solve 4-Queens and print all solutions


Solve subset sum / permutation problems



Tips for Teaching First-Term Students


Start with an intuitive story (maze or N-Queens)


Draw the decision tree on the board


Show how recursion + backtracking explores the tree


Show stack frames for recursive calls to visualize undoing choices


Give a small code example they can run live

Absolutely! Here’s a set of full lecture notes you can say when teaching “When to use recursion”, structured clearly for first-term students. I’ll include explanations, examples, and ways to emphasize the concepts.

When to Use Recursion

1. Simplicity and Readability
Key Idea:
Recursion can make code shorter, cleaner, and easier to understand when a problem can be naturally divided into smaller subproblems.
Example: Factorial
Iterative:
int factorial(int n) {
    int result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) result *= i;
    return result;
}
Recursive:
int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}


Recursive version is more readable and mirrors the mathematical definition.


Shows direct translation of problem logic into code.


Teaching Tip:

“Recursion lets you write code that looks like the problem statement itself.”


2. Natural Fit for Certain Problems
Key Idea:
Some problems are inherently hierarchical or recursive, meaning they break down naturally into smaller instances of the same problem.
Common examples:


Tree Traversals: Binary trees, decision trees


Divide and Conquer: Merge Sort, Quick Sort


Backtracking: N-Queens, Sudoku, maze solving


Combinatorial problems: Generating permutations, combinations, subsets


Example: Fibonacci


Recursive version is directly based on the definition: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)


Iterative version needs extra variables and bookkeeping, making it slightly less obvious.


Teaching Tip:

“If the problem is defined in terms of smaller subproblems, recursion is often the natural choice.”


3. Natural Use of Stack
Key Idea:
Recursion automatically uses the call stack to store intermediate states.


Each function call pauses the current state and resumes later.


You don’t need to manually manage a stack or queue.


Example: Depth-First Search (DFS) in a graph


Recursive DFS implicitly keeps track of the path and visited nodes on the call stack.


Iterative DFS requires explicit stack management.


Teaching Tip:

“Recursion is like having the computer automatically manage the stack for you. Each call remembers where it left off.”


4. Summary for Students





















AdvantageExplanationSimplicity & ReadabilityMakes code shorter, mirrors problem definition, easier to understand.Natural Fit for Certain ProblemsWorks best with divide-and-conquer, hierarchical, or combinatorial problems.Uses Stack AutomaticallySaves you from manually managing state or bookkeeping.
Speaker Notes:

“Recursion is not always the fastest or most memory-efficient, but it’s incredibly useful when:


the problem can be divided into similar subproblems


clarity and readability are more important than tiny performance gains


the solution naturally fits a tree-like or hierarchical structure.”




5. Optional Demo / Visual


Show recursive vs iterative factorial.


Show DFS recursion on a small graph vs iterative DFS with a manual stack.


Highlight how the call stack automatically keeps track of state.

Below is a clear, concise, exam-oriented explanation with small C++ code examples.

1. Memory areas in a C++ program
A running C++ program typically uses these memory regions:
1. Text / Code Segment

Stores compiled machine instructions
Read-only
Shared among processes

int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

2. Global / Static Storage Area


Stores:


Global variables


static variables (global and local)




Allocated once, exists for entire program lifetime


int globalVar = 10;
 
void f() {
    static int counter = 0;
    counter++;
}

3. Stack


Stores:


Function parameters


Local (automatic) variables


Return addresses




Managed automatically (LIFO)


Fast, limited size


void foo() {
    int x = 5;   // on stack
}

4. Heap (Free Store)


Used for dynamic memory allocation


Manually managed (new/delete, malloc/free)


Larger but slower than stack


int* p = new int(10);  // heap
delete p;

5. BSS Segment


Stores uninitialized global/static variables


Zero-initialized by default


int x;        // global → BSS
static int y; // static → BSS

2. Types of program data in C++
This classification is about storage duration.

1. Automatic Storage (automatic variables)


Default for local variables


Stored on stack


Lifetime: block scope


void f() {
    int a = 10;   // automatic
}

2. Static Storage


Exists for entire program execution


Includes:


Global variables


static local variables




Stored in global/static area


static int x = 5;
 
void f() {
    static int y = 10;
}

3. Dynamic Storage


Allocated at runtime


Stored on heap


Lifetime controlled manually


int* p = new int(20);
delete p;

4. Thread-local Storage (C++11+)


One instance per thread


Lifetime: thread execution


thread_local int counter = 0;

3. Summary Table



































CategoryStored WhereCreated WhenDestroyed WhenAutomaticStackBlock entryBlock exitStaticGlobal/Static areaProgram startProgram endDynamicHeapnew/mallocdelete/freeThread-localTLSThread startThread end

4. Common interview trap ⚠️
int* f() {
    int x = 10;
    return &x;  // ❌ dangling pointer (stack memory)
}
Correct:
int* f() {
    int* x = new int(10);
    return x;   // caller must delete
}

Below is a straightforward, no-fluff explanation, aligned with systems / C++ fundamentals, with code where useful.

1. Why can’t we have dynamic-sized data on the stack?
Short answer: the stack must be predictable and fast.
Key reasons


Stack allocation is compile-time–based


Size of stack variables must be known at compile time


Enables simple pointer moves (SP -= size)




int n;
cin >> n;
int arr[n];   // ❌ NOT standard C++ (GCC allows as extension)
Why this is bad for stack:


Stack frame size would be unknown until runtime


Breaks fast, deterministic stack management




Stack uses fixed-size stack frames



Each function call creates a stack frame


Frame layout is known at compile time


void f() {
    int a;
    double b;
}
Compiler knows exactly how much stack to reserve.


Unbounded growth is dangerous



Stack has limited size


Allowing dynamic expansion per variable → easy stack overflow


void f() {
    int huge[1'000'000]; // ❌ likely stack overflow
}

2. Why does the heap exist?
The heap exists to solve what the stack cannot.
Heap provides:


Runtime-sized allocation


Longer lifetime than a function


Flexible memory management


int n;
cin >> n;
int* arr = new int[n];   // heap ✔
You only know n at runtime → heap is required.

3. Stack vs Heap — core difference








































FeatureStackHeapAllocationAutomaticManualSize knownCompile timeRuntimeSpeedVery fastSlowerLifetimeScope-basedProgrammer-controlledMemory limitSmallLargeAccessLocalGlobal (via pointer)

4. Is stack size determined and static?
Mostly YES.


Stack size is:


Fixed at program start (or thread start)


Determined by:


OS defaults


Linker / runtime settings






Examples:


Linux: often 8 MB


Windows: often 1 MB


Important:


Stack does not resize dynamically


Once full → stack overflow



5. What happens when a function is called?
Step-by-step:


Arguments are pushed


Return address is saved


New stack frame is created


Local variables are allocated


➡️ Yes, stack size changes (grows).
void f() {
    int x;
}
 
void g() {
    int y;
    f();
}
Call sequence:
main()
 └── g()
      └── f()

Each call:


Pushes a new stack frame


Moves the stack pointer



Visual example
|            | ← higher addresses
|  f frame   |
|------------|
|  g frame   |
|------------|
| main frame |
|------------|
|            | ← lower addresses

When f() returns:


Its stack frame is popped


Stack pointer moves back



6. Why stack allocation is so fast?
Because allocation is just:
SP = SP - frame_size
Deallocation:
SP = SP + frame_size
No searching, no bookkeeping.
Heap needs:


Metadata


Free lists


Fragmentation handling



7. Important misconception ❌

“Dynamic memory can’t exist on the stack”

❌ Wrong.
What can’t exist:

Dynamically sized allocations

What can exist:
int* p = new int(10); // pointer on stack


p → stack


*p → heap



8. One-line intuition (good for exams)


Stack: fast, fixed, short-lived


Heap: flexible, dynamic, long-lived

Below are precise, low-level answers, no hand-waving.

1. How does GCC allow Variable Length Arrays (VLAs)?
Do they use heap?
Short answer
No, VLAs do NOT use the heap.
GCC allocates them on the stack at runtime.

What standard C++ says


C++ does NOT support VLAs


GCC allows them as a non-standard extension


int n;
cin >> n;
int a[n];   // ❌ not standard C++, ✔ GCC extension

How GCC implements VLAs
GCC uses dynamic stack allocation, typically via:


alloca


or direct stack pointer adjustment


Conceptually:
read n
size = n * sizeof(int)
SP = SP - size   // reserve stack memory at runtime
This memory:


Is still stack memory


Is freed automatically when the function returns



Why this is dangerous
void f() {
    int n = 1'000'000;
    int a[n];   // stack overflow risk
}


Stack has fixed limit


Large VLAs → crash


This is why C++ standard forbids VLAs.

2. Stack overflow vs Heap overflow
Stack Overflow
Cause


Too many function calls


Very large local variables


Infinite recursion


void f() {
    int a[1000000];
}
or
void recurse() {
    recurse();
}
What happens


Stack pointer crosses stack boundary


OS raises segmentation fault / access violation



Heap Overflow
Two meanings (important!)
(A) Writing past allocated heap memory (most common)
int* p = new int[5];
p[10] = 42;   // ❌ heap buffer overflow


Overwrites adjacent heap memory


Causes undefined behavior


Security vulnerability



(B) Heap exhaustion (less common term)
while (true) {
    new int[1000000];
}


Heap runs out of memory


new throws std::bad_alloc



Comparison






























FeatureStack OverflowHeap OverflowHappens whenStack limit exceededMemory corruption or exhaustionTypical causeRecursion, large localsOut-of-bounds writeDetectabilityImmediate crashSilent corruptionSecurity riskLowHigh

3. Does the program know at line 1 that a variable will be created at line 1000?
Short answer
Yes — the compiler knows, but the program at runtime does not “predict the future.”
Let’s separate compile time and runtime.

Compile time (compiler’s view)
The compiler:


Parses the entire function


Knows all local variables


Computes stack frame layout


void f() {
    int a;
    // ...
    int b;
}
Compiler knows:


a and b both belong to the same stack frame


Memory for both is reserved when f() is entered


Even if b is at line 1000.

Runtime (actual execution)
At runtime:


Stack frame is created once, at function entry


All locals exist immediately


void f() {
    int a;   // memory already reserved
    // ...
    int b;   // memory already reserved
}
➡️ Line number is irrelevant to memory allocation.

Exception: GCC VLAs
void f() {
    int n;
    cin >> n;
    int a[n];  // size known only at runtime
}
Here:


Stack size is adjusted during execution


Compiler emits runtime stack growth code


This breaks normal guarantees → why VLAs are non-standard.

4. Key takeaways (exam-ready)


GCC VLAs:


Allocated on stack


Implemented via runtime stack pointer adjustment


Not heap


Non-standard in C++




Stack overflow:


Stack limit exceeded


Immediate crash




Heap overflow:


Writing beyond heap allocation


Silent corruption, security risk




Stack allocation:


Compiler knows all locals at compile time


Memory reserved when function starts, not line-by-line

Let’s answer this very concretely, step by step, with no vague metaphors.

1. Where does &a point to exactly?
int a = 10;
cout << &a;
a is a local automatic variable
➡️ It lives on the stack
So &a is:

A virtual memory address inside the stack segment of this process.

❌ Not:


the base of RAM


the base of your program file


✔️ It is an address in your process’s virtual address space.

2. Virtual address vs RAM (very important)
The address printed (e.g. 0x7ffd3c2a4abc) is:


A virtual address


Meaningful only inside your program


Translated by the MMU (hardware) using page tables


Your program
   |
virtual address (0x7ffd...)
   |
MMU
   |
physical RAM (unknown to you)

➡️ You never see real RAM addresses in user programs.

3. Is this address relative to the base of the program?
No.
Your process memory layout looks like:
High addresses
-----------------
Stack  ← &a is here
-----------------
Heap
-----------------
Globals / static
-----------------
Code (text)
-----------------
Low addresses



The address is absolute in virtual memory


Not relative to code, not relative to main, not relative to RAM



4. Can I add to this address and go outside my program?
Technically: YES
Legally / safely: NO ❌
int* p = &a;
p = p + 1000;
cout << *p;   // ❌ undefined behavior
What happens?


You might:


Access another stack variable


Hit protected memory


Crash (segmentation fault)


Corrupt data silently




Why?


OS enforces memory protection


Accessing memory outside allowed pages → crash



5. Does C++ stop you from doing this?
No.
C++ trusts you:


Pointer arithmetic is allowed


Bounds checking is your responsibility



6. Is there a way to visually debug memory?
YES — several ways

1️⃣ Using a debugger (GDB)
Compile with debug info:
g++ -g main.cpp
gdb ./a.out
Inside gdb:
break main
run
print &a
x/16xb &a     # examine 16 bytes from &a
This shows raw memory bytes.

2️⃣ AddressSanitizer (BEST for learning)
g++ -fsanitize=address -g main.cpp


Detects:


Stack overflow


Heap overflow


Use-after-free




Shows exact memory layout + error



3️⃣ Valgrind (Linux)
valgrind ./a.out


Slower


Extremely detailed heap/stack reports



4️⃣ Visual debuggers (IDE)


CLion


Visual Studio


VS Code + GDB


They show:


Stack frames


Addresses


Memory view window



7. Is a an automatic variable?
YES ✔️
int a = 10;
Properties:


Storage duration: automatic


Memory: stack


Lifetime: entry → exit of main


Equivalent:
auto int a = 10;  // same thing

8. What happens when main returns?


Stack frame destroyed


Address of a becomes invalid


Any pointer to a becomes dangling


int* p;
{
    int a = 10;
    p = &a;
}
cout << *p;   // ❌ undefined behavior

Yes — the heap can change size, but it does not break your program’s memory layout or addresses. Let me explain carefully.

1. Heap growth and memory layout
Typical process virtual memory layout (Linux x86_64):
High addresses
-----------------
Stack      ↑
           grows downward
-----------------
Heap       ↑
           grows upward
-----------------
BSS / Data
-----------------
Text (code)
Low addresses



Heap and stack grow toward each other.


Text/code and static/global areas are fixed.


Heap can expand, but only within its allocated virtual memory region.



How heap grows


Initial heap region is set by OS loader


When you do:


int* p = new int[100000];


C++ runtime (operator new) asks the OS for more memory if needed


Linux: via brk/sbrk or mmap


Windows: via VirtualAlloc



Addresses of old allocations do not change, unless you explicitly move them (e.g., std::vector reallocating).


2. Does heap growth change addresses in other segments?
No.


Text segment: fixed in memory


Stack: fixed base, grows downward


Globals/statics: fixed


Heap growth is handled by the OS giving virtual pages, usually far from other segments.


Virtual memory = each process gets its own address space


OS manages page tables so your code sees a consistent layout



3. How std::vector manages dynamic resizing
std::vector<int> v;
v.push_back(1); 
v.push_back(2); 


Vector allocates heap memory


If it runs out of space, it:


Allocates new larger memory block on heap


Copies old elements


Deletes old block




Addresses of previous elements may change


But stack, code, globals stay untouched



4. Key points about addresses


Stack, code, globals have fixed addresses.


Heap can grow or shrink dynamically.


Virtual memory ensures no collisions.


OS maintains mapping using page tables — you never see physical RAM addresses.



5. Visual analogy (virtual memory map)
Address space (virtual) ↑
+------------------+
| Stack            |
|                  |
|                  |
+------------------+  ← Stack base
| Heap             | grows ↑
+------------------+
| BSS / Data       |
+------------------+
| Text / Code      |
+------------------+
0x00000000         ← Low addresses



Heap expansion = OS mapping more pages above current heap


Stack never moves until function calls push frames


Segments never collide; OS enforces limits



✅ Summary

Heap can grow dynamically
Growth does not shift code or stack
Virtual memory ensures addresses remain valid
Stack and static/global areas stay fixed
Only heap allocations that move (like vector reallocation) change addresses for that block

Let’s break this down carefully — it’s a classic source of confusion in C++.

1. Stack layout for multiple variables
int a = 1;
int b = 2;
int c = 3;


These are automatic (stack) variables


Compiler assigns offsets in the stack frame


Usually you’ll see addresses that are close together


But “exactly contiguous” is not guaranteed



Example (typical debug run)
&a = 0x7ffee3b2c9ac
&b = 0x7ffee3b2c9a8
&c = 0x7ffee3b2c9a4



The addresses are 4 bytes apart (on x86_64 int = 4 bytes)


Looks contiguous, but note the addresses are descending because stack grows downward



2. Why they might not be exactly contiguous


Alignment / padding


CPUs often require variables to start at addresses multiple of their size (4 or 8 bytes)


Compiler may insert padding to satisfy alignment




Optimization


Compiler may reorder variables to improve performance


Some variables may be stored in registers instead of stack




Debug vs Release builds


Debug: more likely to see contiguous addresses


Release: compiler may reorder or optimize away





Example with padding
char x;
int y;


x may occupy 1 byte


y may need 4-byte alignment → 3 bytes padding added


Memory layout:


Offset 0: x
Offset 1-3: padding
Offset 4-7: y


So not exactly back-to-back in memory


3. Heap allocations
int* p = new int;
int* q = new int;


Each new allocates independently on the heap


Addresses may be far apart, not contiguous



4. Key takeaway


Stack automatic variables are usually close together


Not guaranteed to be exactly contiguous


Alignment, padding, compiler optimizations, and CPU architecture affect exact placement


C++ standard does not guarantee any particular order or adjacency



✅ Quick rule of thumb for exams:

“Variables declared consecutively may be stored near each other, but exact adjacency is not guaranteed due to alignment and compiler optimizations.”

1. What is padding?


Padding is extra unused bytes added by the compiler to satisfy memory alignment requirements.


CPUs read/write memory faster if data is aligned on certain boundaries (4 or 8 bytes).


Without padding, misaligned access can slow down the program or even crash on some architectures.



Example: alignment with int on x86_64
struct Example {
    char c;   // 1 byte
    int x;    // 4 bytes
};
Memory layout:
Offset 0: c
Offset 1-3: padding (to align 'x')
Offset 4-7: x



sizeof(Example) = 8 bytes, not 5


Padding ensures x is at address divisible by 4



Why padding exists


CPU alignment requirements

int usually requires 4-byte alignment



Performance optimization

Misaligned accesses may be slower



Consistency across platforms



2. Boolean size


bool in C++ is 1 byte, not 1 bit


Why not 1 bit? CPUs can’t easily address individual bits


Multiple booleans may be packed manually using bit-fields:


struct Flags {
    bool a : 1;
    bool b : 1;
    bool c : 1;
};


a, b, c now use 1 bit each, packed into bytes


Compiler may still pad struct to satisfy alignment

Key points about padding


Each type has alignment requirement


Padding may be inserted before or after variables in structs


Padding is compiler and architecture dependent


Use sizeof() to check actual memory size:


cout << sizeof(S) << endl; // prints 16

Padding = extra bytes added for alignment


bool = 1 byte (cannot be 1 bit individually)


Common type sizes on 64-bit:


bool=1, char=1, short=2, int=4, long=8, long long=8, float=4, double=8, pointer=8


Structs may be larger than sum of members due to padding

Let’s break this down carefully—it’s a subtle topic, but very useful to show students.

1. Address of a function
In C++:


Every function exists somewhere in memory, just like a variable does.


The address of a function is simply the location in memory where the machine code for that function starts.


You can take it using the function name itself, or explicitly with &:


#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
 
void myFunc() {
    cout << "Hello!" << endl;
}
 
int main() {
    void (*ptr)() = myFunc;      // pointer to function
    // or equivalently:
    void (*ptr2)() = &myFunc;    // & is optional for functions
 
    ptr();   // calls myFunc through the pointer
    ptr2();  // same thing
}


ptr is a function pointer.


The type must match the function signature: here void() because myFunc takes nothing and returns void.


✅ So yes, you can use &, but for functions it’s optional. Both myFunc and &myFunc give the address of the function.

2. Size of a pointer


A pointer stores a memory address, regardless of what it points to.


On most modern systems:



















ArchitecturePointer size32-bit4 bytes64-bit8 bytes

The type of the pointer (int*, char*, void*, or function pointer) does not affect its size, only the target type affects how you dereference it.

Example:
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
 
int main() {
    int x;
    int* p = &x;
    void (*fptr)() = nullptr;
 
    cout << "int* size: " << sizeof(p) << endl;
    cout << "function ptr size: " << sizeof(fptr) << endl;
}
On a 64-bit machine, this prints:
int* size: 8
function ptr size: 8


Function pointers may technically differ on some architectures, but on most modern PCs they are also 8 bytes on 64-bit systems.


3. Key points for students


Every function has an address in memory where its machine code resides.


You can store it in a function pointer and call it indirectly.


Pointer size is constant for the architecture, not dependent on the type it points to.

Pointer arithmetic is a very important concept in C++ because pointers aren’t just numbers—they point to types in memory, so arithmetic behaves a bit differently. Let’s go through it carefully.

1. What is pointer arithmetic?
When you add or subtract integers to a pointer, the pointer moves in units of the type it points to, not bytes.
Example:
int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int* p = arr;  // points to arr[0]
 
p = p + 1;     // moves to arr[1], not 1 byte ahead
cout << *p << endl;  // 20


Here p + 1 adds 1 × sizeof(int) bytes to the address.


For char* pointers, p + 1 moves 1 byte (because sizeof(char) = 1).



2. Allowed operations
For a pointer p:





























OperationMeaning / Examplep + nMove n elements forwardp - nMove n elements backwardp1 - p2Distance between two pointers (in elements, not bytes)p++ / ++pMove forward by 1 elementp-- / --pMove backward by 1 element
Important: You can only do meaningful arithmetic within the same array or one past the array.

3. What about *, /, etc.?

* is dereference, not arithmetic:

int x = *p;  // read value at pointer


You cannot do p * n or p / n. Those operations don’t make sense for pointers in C++.


Pointer arithmetic is limited to addition and subtraction, plus comparison operators:


p < q, p > q, p <= q, p >= q, p == q, p != q

Useful for iterating over arrays:

for(int* ptr = arr; ptr < arr + 5; ptr++)
    cout << *ptr << " ";

4. Extra: pointer difference
When you subtract pointers:
int* p1 = &arr[4];
int* p0 = &arr[0];
 
cout << p1 - p0 << endl;  // 4


The result is in number of elements, not bytes.


It’s type-safe, because it knows the size of the element type.



✅ Summary


Allowed: + n, - n, ++, --, pointer subtraction, comparisons


Not allowed: * n, / n (multiply/divide)


* is for dereferencing, not arithmetic

Absolutely! Let’s go step by step—pointers are one of the most confusing but powerful concepts in C++, and understanding them deeply helps students grasp memory, performance, and low-level programming.

1. Why do we need to learn pointers?
Pointers are useful for:


Direct memory access:


Allows you to access and manipulate memory directly, which is essential for system-level programming, embedded systems, or performance-critical code.


Example: dynamic memory allocation (new/delete), manipulating arrays, structs, etc.




Dynamic memory allocation:


Pointers are needed to allocate memory at runtime (heap).


int* arr = new int[10];  // allocate array at runtime
delete[] arr;            // free memory


Efficient data structures:

Linked lists, trees, graphs, hash tables all use pointers to connect nodes.



Function parameters by reference (without copies):


Pass large structs/arrays efficiently.


void modify(int* p) { *p = 10; }
int x = 5;
modify(&x);  // change x directly


Interfacing with hardware / OS:

Low-level languages, drivers, embedded systems often require memory addresses directly.



✅ In short: pointers teach how memory works, which is crucial for C++ and systems programming.

2. Do we have pointers in other languages?


C: Yes, identical to C++.


C++: Full pointers + references.


Rust: Has references and unsafe raw pointers.


Python, Java, JavaScript: No raw pointers; they use references implicitly.


In Python, every variable is a reference to an object.


You can’t do pointer arithmetic or access memory directly.





So C/C++ are the main languages where you need manual pointer management.


3. Different ways of writing pointers in C++
You can declare pointers in slightly different syntaxes, especially where you place the *:
int* p1;   // most common
int *p2;   // also valid
int * p3;  // spaces around *

Important: * binds to the variable name, not the type:

int* a, b;  // a is a pointer, b is an int!

If you want both as pointers:

int *a, *b; // both are pointers

4. Which style is more common / correct?

Most textbooks and C++ developers prefer:

int* p;   // emphasizes "p is a pointer to int"


But it’s largely style preference, as long as you understand that * attaches to the variable, not the type.


Personally, I teach students: use int* p, and if you declare multiple pointers, use separate lines to avoid confusion.

1. new[] (classic C++)
int* arr = new int[5];        // uninitialized
int* arr2 = new int[5]();    // initialized to 0
int* arr3 = new int[5]{1,2,3,4,5}; // list initialization


Memory is contiguous


Size known only at runtime


Must free with:


delete[] arr;

2. malloc (C-style, not recommended in C++)
int* arr = (int*)malloc(5 * sizeof(int));


No constructors


Must free with free(arr)


Do not mix with new/delete



3. std::vector (modern, recommended)
vector<int> arr(5);              // 5 zeros
vector<int> arr2 = {1,2,3,4,5};


Heap allocated internally


Automatic cleanup


Safer, preferred in real C++



2️⃣ 2D array allocation on the heap
There are three main ways.

🔹 Method 1: Array of pointers (rows allocated separately)
int rows = 3, cols = 4;
 
int** arr = new int*[rows];
for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++) {
    arr[i] = new int[cols];
}
Access:
arr[i][j] = 10;
Deallocation:
for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++) {
    delete[] arr[i];
}
delete[] arr;
Characteristics:


Rows not contiguous


Flexible row sizes


More allocations


Common in teaching pointers



🔹 Method 2: Single contiguous block (pointer arithmetic)
int rows = 3, cols = 4;
 
int* arr = new int[rows * cols]();
Access:
arr[i * cols + j] = 10;
Deallocation:
delete[] arr;
Characteristics:


Fully contiguous memory


Cache-friendly


Slightly harder indexing


Very common in performance code



🔹 Method 3: Pointer to array (true 2D layout)
int rows = 3, cols = 4;
 
int (*arr)[4] = new int[rows][4];
Access:
arr[i][j] = 10;
Deallocation:
delete[] arr;
Characteristics:


Contiguous


Natural arr[i][j] syntax


Column size must be known at compile time


Closest to stack-based 2D arrays



3️⃣ Initialization examples for 2D heap arrays
Array of pointers:
for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++)
        arr[i][j] = i + j;
Contiguous block:
int* arr = new int[rows * cols]();
(Zero-initialized using ())

4️⃣ delete vs delete[]
This is critical.
delete
int* p = new int;
delete p;


Calls destructor once


Used for single objects



delete[]
int* arr = new int[5];
delete[] arr;


Calls destructor for each element


Used for arrays



❌ Wrong usage (undefined behavior!)
int* arr = new int[5];
delete arr;    // ❌ WRONG
or
int* p = new int;
delete[] p;    // ❌ WRONG

5️⃣ Quick comparison table (great for slides)















































Allocation typeSyntaxContiguousAccessDeallocation1D arraynew int[n]Yesarr[i]delete[]2D (pointer array)int**Noarr[i][j]nested delete[]2D (flat)int*Yesarr[i*cols+j]delete[]2D (true 2D)int (*p)[C]Yesp[i][j]delete[]vectorvector<T>Yesv[i]automatic

6️⃣ Teaching takeaway for students


Stack arrays → simple, fixed size


Heap arrays → dynamic, flexible


Always match new with delete, new[] with delete[]


Prefer std::vector in real projects


Learn raw pointers to understand memory, not to abuse it



If you want, next I can:


draw memory layout diagrams


compare heap vs stack visually


or show common exam traps with pointers and arrays


Just tell me 👍
Good questions. Let’s be precise and correct, because this topic is often explained sloppily.

1. Is “reseated” used correctly here?
Yes — “reseated” is the correct technical term.

Reseating a reference means:
making the reference refer to a different object after initialization.

In C++:


References cannot be reseated


Pointers can be reseated


Example:
int a = 1, b = 2;
 
int& r = a;   // bind reference
r = b;        // ❌ NOT reseating
This does NOT reseat r.
It assigns the value of b to a.
To reseat (which is impossible for references):
// r = &b;  ❌ invalid
Pointers:
int* p = &a;
p = &b;   // ✔ reseating pointer

2. What is a reference variable?
A reference is an alias for an existing object.
int x = 10;
int& r = x;


r is not a separate object


r is another name for x


r = 20;
cout << x;  // 20

3. Core properties of references (with code)

3.1 References must be initialized
✔️ Correct.
int x = 10;
int& r = x;   // ok
 
int& r2;      // ❌ error
Pointers:
int* p;       // allowed (but dangerous)

3.2 References cannot be reseated
✔️ Correct.
int a = 1, b = 2;
int& r = a;
 
r = b;   // assigns b to a


r still refers to a


a becomes 2



3.3 References must always refer to an object
✔️ Mostly correct, with nuance.
int& r = x;   // must bind to something


Cannot be null


Cannot be uninitialized


But this is not enforced at runtime:
int* p = nullptr;
int& r = *p;   // ❌ undefined behavior
So:


References can dangle


They are not magically safe



3.4 Pointers can point to nothing
✔️ Correct.
int* p = nullptr;
This is a valid state for pointers.

4. Are references “safe”?
⚠️ This statement is only partially true

“References are safe (outside of dangling references)”

What references ARE safe from:


Null checks


Accidental reseating


Forgetting initialization


What references are NOT safe from:


Dangling references


Lifetime issues


Aliasing bugs


Example of dangling reference:
int& f() {
    int x = 10;
    return x;   // ❌ dangling reference
}

5. References vs Pointers — Correct Comparison Table













































FeatureReferencePointerMust be initialized✔️ Yes❌ NoCan be null❌ No✔️ YesCan be reseated❌ No✔️ YesHas its own identity❌ No✔️ YesCan be dangling✔️ Yes✔️ YesSyntax overheadLowHigherTypical useAlias / parameterOwnership, dynamic memory

6. Common and correct use cases for references

6.1 Function parameters (most important use)
Avoids copying, guarantees valid object.
void increment(int& x) {
    x++;
}
int a = 5;
increment(a);

6.2 Const references (read-only access)
void print(const std::string& s) {
    cout << s << endl;
}


Avoids copying


Prevents modification



6.3 Return references (advanced, careful!)
int& getElement(int arr[], int i) {
    return arr[i];   // safe if array outlives reference
}

6.4 Operator overloading
class Vec {
public:
    int x;
    int& operator[](int i) {
        return x;
    }
};

6.5 Range-based for loops
for (int& x : vec) {
    x *= 2;
}

7. When to use pointers instead
Use pointers when you need:


Optional value (nullptr)


Reseating


Dynamic allocation


Polymorphism / ownership


Low-level memory control


void process(int* p) {
    if (!p) return;
    *p = 10;
}

8. Final corrected version of your statements
✔️ All are correct, with this refined wording:

References must be initialized; pointers are not required to be initialized (but should be).
References cannot be reseated; pointers can be reseated.
References must be bound to an object; pointers may be null.
References reduce certain classes of errors but can still dangle and are not inherently safe.


One-sentence rule (very good to remember)

Use references by default for function parameters; use pointers when “no object” or reseating is a valid state.

If you want next:


Reference vs pointer at assembly level


Why references exist at all (compiler design)


Why std::optional<T> replaces some pointer use cases

C++ Basic Programming – TA Team Initiative
Welcome to the C++ Basic Programming Course Repository — a comprehensive, community-driven learning resource.
This project is more than a collection of materials — it’s a living documentation of how our teaching team collaborates, mentors, and builds a hands-on learning experience for students.

Purpose and Vision
Our mission is to ensure that every student not only understands C++ concepts but can also apply them confidently through coding, problem-solving, and projects.
We believe that learning to code should be an active, guided process — not a passive one.
To achieve that, we combine theory from lectures with practice, mentorship, and structured documentation.

What This Repository Contains





















SectionDescription/overview/Conceptual overviews for each lecture week — theory summaries, examples, and key takeaways./workshops/Hands-on guided activities for each topic, designed to help students learn by doing./assignments/Weekly assignments that reinforce lecture material and build problem-solving skills.
All sections are written in Markdown, making them easy to read, modify, and publish (e.g., on GitHub Pages or Quartz).

Our Teaching Model
Our approach combines theoretical coverage, active practice, and close mentorship:


Weekly Lectures

Delivered by the professor.
Introduce core programming concepts in C++.



Workshops

Designed and run by TAs.
Translate concepts into hands-on coding experiences.
Encourage collaboration and experimentation.



Assignments

Weekly exercises that challenge students to apply what they’ve learned.
Reviewed and discussed with mentors.



Mentorship

Each TA mentors a small group of students.
Provides personalized support, code reviews, and guidance.
Builds a feedback loop between students, TAs, and the professor.




Why We Document This
We’re documenting everything we do for three major reasons:


Comprehensiveness for Learners
Provide a high-quality, public resource for current students and self-learners outside the university.


Pedagogical Transparency
Allow educators and future TA teams to see and improve upon our structure, methods, and materials.


Continuity and Growth
Leave behind a foundation that future teaching teams or other institutions can build upon, adapt, and evolve.



Course Topics Overview





























































































WeekTopicDescriptionOverviewWorkshopAssignment1Algorithmic Thinking & Problem-SolvingDevelop foundational skills in algorithm design: representing problems with flowcharts and pseudocode, and reasoning about step-by-step solutions.Overview-Assignment2Introduction to C++ & Basic Programming Constructs & Data TypesGet started with C++: setting up the IDE, basic syntax, compiling and linking, and simple programs. Understand fundamental data types, expressions and operationsOverviewWorkshopAssignment3Control StructuresMove into control flow with logical operators, if/else, switch, loops, iteration and avoiding infinite loops.OverviewWorkshopAssignment4Functions & Modular DesignLearn how to design and call functions in C++, including void vs return-type, parameter passing, overloading, and thinking in modular pieces.OverviewWorkshopAssignment5Arrays, Strings & Multidimensional DataExplore static arrays, C++ strings and multidimensional data structures. Incorporate memory-thinking in simple data manipulations.6Advanced Functions & RecursionDeepen function usage with recursion, higher-level thinking about how functions call themselves, and problem-solving patterns that leverage recursion.7Pointers & Dynamic MemoryDive into pointers, dynamic memory allocation/deallocation (e.g., new, delete), pointer arithmetic, and how memory model impacts correct usage of arrays/strings.8File I/O, Structs & A Very Brief Introduction to Object-Oriented ConceptsWork with file input/output streams, define and use structs, and get a first glance at OOP mindset9Mini ProjectIntegrate the learned topics into a hands-on project: design, implement, test a moderately sized application showcasing applied algorithms, data structures and modular code.10Final Project & Wrap-upLaunch the final project with full guidelines: design documentation, coding standards, testing, and presentation. Wrap up with reflections and next steps in C++ or software development.

Long-Term Goals

Create a sustainable, evolving educational model that balances theory and practice.
Encourage open-source education — anyone can learn from or contribute to our materials.
Serve as a baseline for future educators in teaching programming effectively.


The Team

Head Teaching Assistant: Mehrdad Shirvani

Contributing
We welcome contributions — whether you’re a TA, a student, or an educator from another institution.
If you’d like to:

Improve explanations or examples
Add new workshop exercises
Suggest assignment ideas
Translate materials

Please open a pull request or contact us.

Tech Stack

GitHub Pages / Quartz for deploying the website

❓ Question 1

Question: “Where are Variable Length Arrays (arrays sized using a runtime variable) allowed in C++ and where are they not?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


Variable Length Arrays (VLAs) are not allowed in standard C++.
C++ requires the size of a built-in array to be a constant expression known at compile time.




❌ Not acceptable in standard C++ (C++11/14/17/20/23/…):
int n = 5;
int arr[n];   // Not valid C++

✔️ Acceptable in standard C (since C99): C allows VLAs.
✔️ Allowed in GCC as an extension, but not portable and not standard.
Reference:
GCC documentation: gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Variable-Length.html
C++ restriction explanation: www.geeksforgeeks.org/why-variable-length-array-were-removed-in-cpp/


❓ Question 2

Question: “Is it valid to use a Variable Length Array when compiling with GCC? In which situations is it not valid?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


GCC does allow VLAs in C++ mode, but only as a non-standard compiler extension.



✔️ OK in GCC when:


Used inside functions (automatic storage):
int n = 10;
int arr[n];   // GCC accepts, but non-standard


❌ Not OK when:


Writing portable or standards-compliant C++


Using MSVC, Clang with strict mode, or compilers that reject VLAs


Using strict flags:


-std=c++20 -pedantic


-Wvla


-Werror




GCC reference:
gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Variable-Length.html

❓ Question 3

Question: “Why are Variable Length Arrays considered unacceptable or non-standard in C++?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


VLAs are rejected by the C++ standard for several reasons:





Compile-time determinism
C++ requires array sizes to be known at compile time for built-in arrays.


Portability issues
Many compilers (MSVC, strict Clang modes) do not support VLAs at all.


Safety considerations
Runtime-sized stack arrays risk unpredictable stack usage and stack overflow.


C++ philosophy
C++ encourages using RAII containers (std::vector, std::array) instead of raw arrays with runtime sizes.


Reference:
www.geeksforgeeks.org/why-variable-length-array-were-removed-in-cpp/

❓ Question 4

Question: “Can const or constexpr be used to provide a size for arrays in C++ when the goal is to avoid Variable Length Arrays?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


Yes — but only if the value is a compile-time constant expression.



✔️ Allowed:
constexpr int N = 10;
int arr[N];   // Valid C++
⚠️ Not allowed:
int n = get_input();
const int x = n; 
int arr[x];        // Still NOT valid — not a constant expression
Summary:

constexpr → always compile-time constant → valid for array sizes
const → not enough unless initialized with a compile-time constant
For real runtime sizes, use std::vector.

Reference:
en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/array
❓ Question

Question: “How are arrays passed to functions in C++? Is it allowed?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


Yes, it is allowed.
In C++, when you pass a built-in array to a function, the array decays into a pointer to its first element.
Example:



void foo(int arr[]) { }     // arr becomes int*
void foo(int* arr) { }      // same thing
So even though an array looks like it’s being passed, the function receives only a pointer, not the entire array.
Reference: en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/array

❓ Question 2

Question: “Are arrays passed by reference or by value?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


A raw array parameter is never passed by value.
The array decays to a pointer → this behaves like pass-by-pointer, not value.





❌ Not pass-by-value (copying an entire array is not what happens)


✔️ Effectively pass-by-reference (because the pointer can modify the original array)


If you do want pass-by-value semantics, you must use something like:
void foo(std::array<int, 5> arr);  // Copies the entire array
Reference: en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/array

❓ Question 3

Question: “Can you control this behavior? Can you pass arrays by value or by reference explicitly?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


Yes — but only using references or std::array.



✔️ Pass entire array by reference (preserves size):
void foo(int (&arr)[5]);   // Reference to array of 5 ints
✔️ Pass entire array by value (copies the whole array):
void foo(std::array<int,5> arr);  // Copy
✔️ Pass entire array by reference (modern way):
void foo(const std::array<int,5>& arr);
❌ You cannot pass a built-in array by value directly.
The syntax does not exist in C++.
Reference: en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/references

❓ Question 4

Question: “Should you specify the size of arrays when passing them? For 1D, 2D, 3D, etc.?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


It depends on the declaration style.



⭐ 1D arrays
You do not specify the size:
void foo(int arr[]);     // OK
void foo(int* arr);      // Same
⭐ Multi-dimensional (2D, 3D, …) arrays
All inner dimensions must be known:
void foo(int arr[][5]);        // OK
void foo(int arr[3][5]);       // OK
void foo(int arr[][5][10]);    // Higher dimensions OK
But the first dimension may be left unspecified because it becomes a pointer:
arr → pointer to an array of 5 ints

Reference: en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/array

❓ Question 5

Question: “Can you use variables as sizes in function parameters? In standard C++ and GCC?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                

✔️ Standard C++

NOT allowed:
Inner dimensions must be compile-time constants.

void foo(int arr[][n]);     // ❌ Not standard C++
✔️ GCC (as extension)

GCC allows Variable Length Arrays (VLA) in function parameters.

void foo(int n, int arr[][n]);   // ✔️ GCC extension
But this is non-portable and not valid standard C++.
References:

Standard rule: en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/array
GCC VLA extension: gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Variable-Length.html


❓ Question 6

Question: “What are the different notations for passing arrays to functions?”



                  
                   Answer
                  
                


C++ supports several styles:



1️⃣ Pointer style
void foo(int* arr);
2️⃣ Array style (decays to pointer)
void foo(int arr[]);
void foo(int arr[10]);    // Size ignored by compiler
3️⃣ Multi-dimensional
void foo(int arr[][5]);
4️⃣ Reference to array (preserves actual size)
void foo(int (&arr)[10]);
5️⃣ Using std::array (recommended for fixed sizes)
void foo(std::array<int,10>& arr);
6️⃣ Using std::vector (recommended for dynamic sizes)
void foo(std::vector<int>& arr);
Reference: en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container
❓ Question: Can you somehow preserve an array’s size and use it in functions?

Answer
Yes — but only if you pass the array in a way that preserves its compile-time size. By default, when you pass a built-in C-style array to a function, it “decays” into a pointer (so size information is lost). (GeeksforGeeks)

If you want to preserve the size, you can pass by reference to an array. Example:
void func(int (&arr)[10]) {
   // Here, sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) works: size = 10.
}
Because arr is a reference to an array of 10 ints, the function knows the array’s size at compile time. (GeeksforGeeks)
If you need a function that works for arrays of any compile-time-known size, you can use a template:
template <size_t N>
void func(int (&arr)[N]) {
   // N is deduced; you can use it inside the function
}
This way the function “remembers” the array size. This pattern avoids the “decay to pointer” problem. (CodeArchPedia.com)
Alternatively, many modern C++ codebases avoid raw arrays and instead use container types (e.g. std::array, std::vector) which carry size information or allow querying their size. (xeverous.github.io)

❓ Question: How to initialize an array to all zeros? — in 1D, 2D, 3D, etc.

Answer



For a 1D built-in array in C++, you can zero-initialize like:
int arr[5] = {0};  // all 5 elements become 0
(GitLab)


For multi-dimensional (2D, 3D, …) built-in arrays, you can do nested brace initialization (or rely on partial zero initialization). For example:
int mat[3][4] = {0};   // all elements become 0
Or for 3D:
int cube[2][3][4] = {0};
The {0} initializes the first element to zero, and all other elements are zero-initialized by default (aggregate initialization rules). (GitLab)


Similarly, if you use std::array, you can zero-initialize:
std::array<int,5> arr = {0};
All members will be zero-initialized. (magodo’s blog)


So yes — you can initialize multi-dimensional arrays (1D, 2D, 3D, etc.) to zero with a simple initializer (or nested braces).

❓ Question: Why is there no compile-time error when you access out-of-bounds in a built-in array (i.e. “out of index”)?

Answer
Because built-in (C-style) arrays in C++ do not perform any bounds checking. The language simply allows arr[i] for any i, and does not verify at runtime whether i is valid. Accessing outside the allocated bounds is undefined behavior. (GitLab)

That means the compiler does not generate an error or warning (in general) if you index beyond the array’s size — it’s up to the programmer to ensure correctness. This is a known risk of raw arrays. (Stack Overflow)
Because of this inherent unsafety (lack of bounds checking, size information lost when passing arrays, no easy way to return raw arrays, etc.), many C++ developers prefer safer alternatives (see below). (Stack Overflow)

❓ Question: What is the “standard array” (i.e. std::array)? What are the differences between std::array and built-in arrays? When is it best to use it?

Answer
std::array<T, N> is a template class in C++ standard library representing a fixed-size array of N elements of type T. It behaves like a thin wrapper over a built-in array, but with advantages. (xeverous.github.io)

Differences / Advantages compared to built-in arrays:


No “decay to pointer” when passed to functions: std::array keeps size information. If you pass std::array<int,5> to a function by value or by reference, the size is known and preserved. (xeverous.github.io)


Supports assignment, copy, move semantics: Unlike built-in arrays (which are not assignable or copyable as a whole), std::array behaves like a regular object. (Stack Overflow)


Has member functions & safer access: For example, .at() performs bounds checking (throws exception on invalid index), while operator [] still gives raw access (no bounds check) — unlike built-in arrays where you only get []. (magodo’s blog)


Interoperability with standard library algorithms: std::array supports iterators, std::begin(), std::end(), which makes it easier to integrate with STL algorithms. (xeverous.github.io)


When is std::array best to use:


When the array size is known at compile time and fixed.


When you want safer semantics — e.g. ability to copy/assign arrays, pass around by value or reference, avoid the “array decay” problems, and optionally get bounds-checked access via .at().


When you want to use standard library features (iterators, algorithms) with array data.


For dynamic or runtime-determined sizes (or if size can change), other types like std::vector, or (since C++20) std::span or dynamic containers are more appropriate. (xeverous.github.io)
